title: Wildlife and protected areas
subtitle: Natural Environment
content:
1. Major Protected Areas & Wildlife Sanctuaries. 
While Nagaland has a relatively small percentage of land under formal government-designated protected areas, its sanctuaries are ecologically vital:   Intanki National Park (Peren District):
Spanning over 200 square kilometers, this is Nagaland's premier national park.
It features dense tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests.
Wildlife: It is home to rare species such as the Hoolock Gibbon, Golden Langur, Sloth Bear, Barking Deer, Wild Buffalo, flying squirrels, and occasionally migrating elephants or tigers. It is also a haven for birdwatchers.   Fakim Wildlife Sanctuary (Kiphire District):
Located close to the Myanmar border near Mount Saramati, this sanctuary covers hilly terrain with sub-tropical and temperate vegetation (including oak, pine, and rhododendron forests).
Wildlife: Famous for housing the rare Blyth's Tragopan (Nagaland’s state bird), Himalayan Palm Civet, barking deer, and diverse pheasants.   Pulie Badze Wildlife Sanctuary (Kohima District):
Situated near the capital city of Kohima, this sanctuary protects the catchment area around the Pulie Badze peak.
Wildlife: Known for serving as a resting and nesting ground for various migratory and resident bird species, including the Blyth's Tragopan.   Rangapahar Wildlife Sanctuary (Dimapur District):
Located in the foothills near Dimapur, this is a smaller sanctuary featuring secondary forests and wetlands, serving as a sanctuary for spotted deer, sambar, and various bird and reptile species.    2. Community Conservation Areas & The "Falcon Capital".
One of Nagaland's most unique environmental success stories is its community-led conservation movement. Because a vast majority of forest land is privately or communally owned by local tribes rather than the government, wildlife protection relies heavily on community initiatives:    Pangti Village & Amur Falcons:
Nagaland (specifically around the Doyang Reservoir in Wokha district) earned international acclaim as the "Amur Falcon Capital of the World."
Millions of migratory Amur falcons stop here on their journey from Siberia to Africa. After historical hunting pressures, local villages (led by Pangti) completely banned hunting and turned into zealous protectors, making it one of the greatest wildlife conservation triumphs globally.
Community Reserved Forests:
Dozens of villages across districts like Zunheboto, Phek, and Mokokchung have set aside portions of their ancestral lands as "Community Conservation Areas" (CCAs) where logging and hunting are strictly prohibited, creating vital biological corridors for wildlife.

title: Forests and biodiversity
subtitle: Natural Environment
content:
Nagaland’s natural environment is defined by its rugged topography, heavy tropical monsoon rainfall, and a high degree of ecological diversity. Situated at the junction of the Indo-Malayan and Indo-Chinese biogeographic realms, the state boasts a remarkably rich assemblage of flora and fauna.
The forests and biodiversity of Nagaland are characterized by the following key aspects:  1. Forest Types & Vegetation Zones.
Because elevation ranges dramatically from the low-lying plains of Dimapur (around 150 meters) to the alpine heights of Mount Saramati (3,840 meters), Nagaland supports a wide spectrum of forest types:
Tropical Evergreen and Semi-Evergreen Forests:
Found primarily in the lower foothills, valleys, and foothills bordering Assam.
These dense, multi-layered forests feature towering trees, thick lianas, orchids, and ferns that thrive in high humidity and warm temperatures.   Sub-Tropical Broadleaf and Pine Forests:
Occupying middle-elevation ranges (roughly 1,000 to 2,000 meters) across districts like Kohima, Wokha, and Mokokchung.
These forests are characterized by a mix of evergreen broadleaf trees (such as oak and chestnut) alongside natural stands of pine.   Temperate and Sub-Alpine Forests:
Found at higher altitudes (above 2,000 meters) near Mount Saramati and high ridges.
Dominated by temperate conifers, rhododendrons, and moss-laden trees.    Bamboo and Grassland Ecosystems:
Bamboo forests cover vast tracts of Nagaland and play a vital role in both the rural economy and local ecology.
Unique high-altitude grasslands, such as those found in the Dzükou Valley, feature rolling meadows interspersed with dwarf bamboo and seasonal wildflowers.    2. Rich Botanical Biodiversity.
Orchids: Nagaland is often referred to as an orchid enthusiast's paradise. It is home to well over 600 species of orchids, ranging from epiphytes clinging to high forest canopy branches to terrestrial varieties on the forest floor.
Rhododendrons: Several species of wild rhododendrons blanket the higher mountain slopes, bursting into bright red and pink blooms during the spring months.
Endemic Flora: The most famous endemic floral species is the Dzükou Lily (Lilium chitrakutense / Lilium species unique to the valley), which blooms exclusively in the marshy grasslands of the Dzükou Valley during the monsoon.   3. Fauna & Wildlife Diversity.
Avifauna (Birds): Nagaland hosts over 500 bird species.
The Blyth’s Tragopan, a rare and stunningly colored horned pheasant, is the state bird.
The state is globally renowned for avian migration, particularly the millions of Amur Falcons that roost around the Doyang Reservoir every autumn. Hornbills (such as the Great Indian Hornbill) are deeply tied to local cultural identity and forest health.
Mammals: The deep forests harbor an array of mammals, including the Hoolock Gibbon, Slow Loris, capped langur, barking deer, wild boar, Himalayan black bear, clouded leopard, and the elusive Serow (a goat-antelope found in rocky, steep terrain). Occasional wild elephants and tigers traverse border foothill corridors.         4. Community-Managed Forests & Conservation Paradigm.
A defining feature of Nagaland's natural environment is that over 85% of the state's forests are privately or communally owned by indigenous clans and villages, rather than managed strictly by the government.
Through traditional governance, local communities have established hundreds of Community Conservation Areas (CCAs).
These self-imposed bans on commercial logging and hunting in designated village reserves have created vital ecological corridors, proving that indigenous community stewardship is a powerful engine for preserving biodiversity.

title: What the Hornbill Festival is
content: The Hornbill Festival - fondly known as the Festival of Festivals - is an annual celebration held in the first week of December at Kisama, Naga Heritage Village, about 12 km from Kohima. A modern-day cultural extravaganza of all Naga tribes, featuring cultural performances, Hornbill Music Festival, traditional sports, food festivals, craft sales, and more.
source: Hornbill Festival 2025 Final Handbook, p. PDF idx 3-4

title: Purpose of the festival
content:
The Hornbill Festival was established by the Government of Nagaland with four primary objectives:  1. Cultural Preservation and Revival
Before the festival's establishment in 2000, many ancient oral traditions, folk music, ritual dances, and indigenous craftsmanship were at risk of fading as younger generations modernized. The festival creates a dedicated annual stage to document, preserve, and pass down this living heritage to future generations. 2. Promoting Inter-Tribal Unity and Interaction
Nagaland is home to over 18 major tribes (and numerous sub-tribes), each with its own distinct language, customs, attire, and local harvest festivals. The Hornbill Festival brings all these diverse communities together under a single umbrella—earning it the title "Festival of Festivals". It fosters cross-cultural dialogue, unity, and mutual respect among tribes that historically lived in isolated hill tracts.  3. Boosting Tourism and Economic Opportunities
The festival serves as Nagaland's primary tourism promotional event. By showcasing the state’s vibrant culture on a global stage, it attracts thousands of domestic and international visitors. This generates sustainable income for local communities, including hospitality providers, artisans, weavers, musicians, tour operators, and food vendors.  4. Bridging Traditional Heritage with Contemporary Expression
While anchored in ancient customs—such as indigenous sports, tribal village life inside traditional wooden huts (Morungs), and folk performances—the festival also embraces modern youth culture. Host events like the Hornbill International Rock Concert, fashion shows, and art exhibitions showcase contemporary Naga talent alongside traditional roots.
source: Hornbill Festival 2025 Final Handbook, and open Source Internet.

title: History and how it began
content:
The Backdrop: Nagaland in the Late 1990s.  By the late 1990s, Nagaland was emerging from decades of political unrest and isolation. While the state possessed an immensely rich, vibrant cultural heritage, passed down orally and preserved across isolated hill tracts by over 16 distinct Naga tribes, there was a growing concern that this unique heritage was slipping away.
The Generational Gap: Modernization, changing lifestyles, and the influence of western education meant younger generations were losing touch with traditional dialects, folk songs, weaving, and indigenous crafts.
Lack of a Unified Platform: While individual tribes had their own major seasonal celebrations (such as the Sekrenyi of the Angami or Moatsu of the Ao), there was no common platform where all Naga tribes could gather to celebrate their shared identity.
Economic Isolation: Tourism to the state was minimal due to past infrastructure and security challenges, meaning local artisans and entrepreneurs had very few avenues to showcase their work to the outside world.  How It Began: December 2000. To address these challenges, the Government of Nagaland, under the leadership of then-Chief Minister Scato Swu and various cultural stakeholders, conceptualized a mega-event.
The Vision: They envisioned a single, grand festival that would showcase the totality of Naga culture, foster harmony and integration among the different tribes, and open the state's doors to tourism.
The Name: It was named the Hornbill Festival after the Indian hornbill, a majestic, highly revered bird deeply symbolic in Naga folklore, songs, and warrior headgear, representing qualities of nobility, beauty, and alertness.
The Inception: The very first Hornbill Festival was held from December 1 to December 10, 2000, coinciding neatly with Nagaland Statehood Day (December 1).  Evolution into the "Festival of Festivals".  What started as a modest state-sponsored cultural meet quickly snowballed into a massive global phenomenon:
The Shift to Kisama: As attendance surged in the early years, the government established the Naga Heritage Village at Kisama (about 12 km from Kohima) specifically as the permanent venue. Modeled after traditional Naga village layouts complete with authentic Morungs (youth dormitories) for each tribe, Kisama gave the festival an immersive, authentic atmosphere.
Global Reach: Over the decades, the festival expanded far beyond tribal dances to incorporate the Hornbill International Rock Contest, art installations, international music acts, literature festivals, and global food pavilions.
Today, what began as a local initiative to preserve fading traditions has successfully transformed into one of South Asia's most famous cultural tourism events, putting Nagaland firmly on the global cultural map.
source: Hornbill Festival 2025 Final Handbook, and open Source Internet.

title: Cultural significance
content:
1. Living Preservation of Naga Heritage.  Oral Tradition Safeguard: Naga history was never written; it was passed down through songs, stories, and rituals. The festival provides an annual living archive where folk songs, war dances, and ancient rituals are performed and kept alive for younger generations.
Symbol of the Hornbill: Named after the revered bird deeply woven into Naga folklore, the festival honors the bird’s symbolic traits grandeur, alertness, and beauty, which are reflected in traditional headgear, attire, and art.  2. A Unifying Platform ("Festival of Festivals").  Inter-Tribal Harmony: Nagaland comprises over 18 distinct tribes with different dialects and traditions. The festival acts as a single, neutral ground where all tribes gather, fostering unity, mutual respect, and cross-cultural understanding.
Authentic Morung Culture: At the Kisama Heritage Village, each tribe builds its own traditional Morung (youth dormitory), displaying its unique architecture, wood carvings, and customs side-by-side.  3. Global Identity and Pride.   Cultural Reclaiming: It shifts the state's global narrative toward its vibrant heritage, craftsmanship, and hospitality.
Bridging Generations: By combining traditional tribal practices with modern music, art, and fashion, it allows young Nagas to celebrate their ancestral roots while expressing contemporary identity.
source: Hornbill Festival 2025 Final Handbook, and open Source Internet.

title: Who organises it
content:
The Hornbill Festival is primarily organized by the State Government of Nagaland.
Executively, the execution and festival management are handled through a joint inter-departmental effort led by government bodies alongside local tribal councils:  Key Organizers & Apex Governing Body.  1. High-Powered Governing Body (Apex Policy Body)  The Government of Nagaland constituted a dedicated High-Powered Governing Body to oversee and direct the festival.
Chairperson: Hon'ble Chief Minister of Nagaland.
Key Members: Deputy Chief Ministers, Cabinet Ministers (Tourism, Horticulture), Advisors for Art & Culture and Industries/Commerce, the Chief Secretary (Member Secretary), and Departmental Secretaries.
Role: Sets the overall strategic vision, policy guidelines, event approvals, site allotments, rate monitoring, and corporate/CSR sponsorships.  2. Nodal Government Departments (Operations)  Department of Tourism: Acts as the primary operational nodal agency for international and domestic tourism promotion, logistics, event scheduling, and hospitality management.
Department of Art & Culture: Manages the authentic presentation of tribal traditions, folk music, ritual dances, literature, and cultural troupe coordination.
Task Force for Music & Arts (TaFMA): Coordinates musical events, concerts, and youth art exhibitions associated with the festival.  3. Tribal Bodies & Local Communities  Naga Tribal Councils (Apex Tribal Bodies): Each participating tribe’s governing council organizes and manages its respective traditional Morung (youth dormitory) at Kisama Heritage Village.
Local Entrepreneurs & Guilds: Local youth groups, artisans, weavers, and culinary associations manage food stalls, craft markets, night carnivals, and transport services in Kohima and Kisama.  4. Supporting Agencies  Ministry of Tourism & Ministry of Culture (Government of India): Provides central backing, funding support, and national promotional outreach.

title: Introduction to Nagaland for visitors
content: Nagaland, often called the "Land of Festivals," is a mountainous state in Northeast India. It is celebrated for its dramatic landscapes, rich indigenous heritage, and warm tribal hospitality.   Key Facts at a Glance:  Capital: Kohima.   Entry Hub: Dimapur (the state's primary airport and railhead).  Official Language: English (Nagamese is widely spoken as the lingua franca).  Core Attractions & Highlights.  Rich Tribal Diversity: Home to over 18 major indigenous tribes (such as the Angami, Ao, Konyak, and Sumi). Each has distinct languages, traditions, vibrant handlooms, and seasonal harvest festivals.    Scenic Trails & Nature: Famous for the Dzüko Valley, trekker's paradise known for rolling green hills and endemic lilies, and Japfü Peak, the state's second-highest summit.   History & Eco-Tourism: Home to Khonoma, India’s first designated green village with a history of British-era resistance, and the Kohima War Cemetery from World War II.   Cuisine: Known for smoked meats, bamboo shoot preparations, local organic greens, and spicy chili varieties (like the Raja Mircha / Ghost Pepper).  Traveler Tip: Domestic Indian tourists require an Inner Line Permit (ILP), while foreign nationals must complete e-FRRO registration prior to entering the state.

title: Angami Tribe
subtitle: Region: Kohima district · Festival: Sekrenyi (also known as Phousanyi)
content:
A major purification festival. Participants are not permitted to work or fight. Observed with elaborate ceremonies, feasting, and traditional attire.

Sekrenyi (also known as Phousanyi) is a major on February 25th. It marks the beginning of the lunar year and focuses on purification and renewal. The festival is especially significant for young men, as it marks their transition from boyhood to adulthood. Key traditions include rituals like Kizie, Zumho, and Dzuseva for purification, and wearing new mhoushü (shawls) and Lohe (traditional attire). Thekra Hie is a celebration where youth gather to enjoy rice beer, meat, and sing traditional songs. The festival also features activities like hunting, gate-pulling (Kharu), and bridge-pulling (Pe), as well as inter- village ceremonies such as Kidakinyi and Vitho. Villagers observe penyie, a break from agricultural work, to focus on the spiritual and cultural aspects of the festival. people.

title: Ao Tribe
subtitle: Region: Mokokchung district · Festival: Moatsü (Moatsü Mong) & Tsüngremmong
content:
The Moatsu Festival (Moatsu Mong) is the primary traditional celebration of the Ao Naga tribe, marking the completion of the sowing season and serving as a vital period for community bonding and cultural preservation.  Celebrated annually in the first week of May, the three-day event transforms agricultural labor into a time of recreation and joy, reinforcing social cohesion through communal feasts, traditional dances, and the lighting of the Sangpangtu (community bonfire). 
Beyond its agricultural roots, the festival holds deep spiritual and social significance, acting as a platform for thanksgiving to deities for a prosperous harvest and for the renewal of social bonds through gift exchange and courtship rituals. It serves as a living archive of Ao heritage, where elders transmit oral histories, folk songs, and values to the younger generation, ensuring the continuity of their distinct cultural identity amidst modernization.

AO Moatsü festival is celebrated by the Ao Naga tribes of Nagaland annually in the first week of May. The Moatsü is the more widely known of the two. It lasts 3 days (May 1–3) and features the Sangpangtu ritual — a large bonfire around which men and women in traditional attire gather to sing, dance, and feast on rice beer and meat.  The village gate is closed so only Ao people attend. Tsüngremmong is considered the biggest Ao festival.  It lasts six days and involves sacrificial offerings (traditionally a pig), prayers to Lijaba (the supreme being), traditional songs, dances, and tug-of-war contests.

title: Chang Tribe
subtitle: Region: Tuensang District · Festival: Naknyulüm/Poanglüm/Kundanglüm
content:
Victory of Good over Evil: The festival is fundamentally a celebration of light's triumph over darkness, symbolizing the moral order and spiritual protection of the community. 
Harvest Thanksgiving: It coincides with the first harvest season, making it both a spiritual and agricultural festival — prayers seek bountiful crops and granary fullness.
Social Cohesion: Despite its solemnity, the festival reinforces kinship through gift exchange, communal feasting, and collective labor (cleaning village paths, wells, and roads on the third day).
Strict Taboos: The festival is governed by rigid observances — no dancing, singing, visitors, marriage, hair-cutting, or construction — underscoring its sacred character. Even a single misstep in ritual is believed to bring famine and pestilence to the village. 
Ancestral Continuity: The Ung clan's elder announces the festival date, preserving a system of clan-based governance and intergenerational knowledge transfer.

Naknyulüm is by far the most prominent.  It is initiated by an elder of the Oungh clan and lasts three days and three nights during the moonless period (Daomao in Chang dialect).  Key rituals include:

Wenshi (Day 1): Women grind pearl millet into flour for steamed biscuits; mithuns and pigs are slaughtered; the scented plant Ngounam is planted around houses to ward off evil. 
Youjem (Day 2): Exchange of food and gifts; top-spinning (yan) competitions for men; Kongkin (bamboo mouth flute) performances by women; a meat-eating contest. 
Nakseeng (Day 3): Village and field paths are cleared; a chicken is released at the village gate by the eldest Oungh clan member to mark the festival's conclusion. 
Notably, no folk dancing or singing takes place during Naknyulüm — the festival is governed by strict ritual observances, and marriages are prohibited for the entire period. Poanglüm: Renewal of friendship ties and treaties with neighbouring communities.  Kundanglüm: A five-day festival tied to jhum (shifting cultivation); the first three days are spent collecting materials for field huts, the huts are collectively built on the fifth day, ending with feasting

title: Konyak Tribe
subtitle: Region: Mon district · Festival: [object Object]
content:
1. Spiritual Blessing & Agricultural FoundationGratitude & Invocations: The agricultural cycle dictates Konyak life. Pre-sowing and spring festivals (like Aoleang) are performed to invoke Kahwang (the supreme deity/God) for fertile soil, timely rains, and seed protection.   Harvest Thanksgiving: Post-harvest festivals (like Lao-ong Mo) serve as collective expressions of gratitude for communal sustenance and survival through another season.2. Preservation of Warrior Identity & HeritageHonoring the Past: The Konyaks are historically famous for being fear-inspiring headhunters and defenders of their land. During major festivals, elders and warriors wear their traditional facial tattoos, brass-skull necklaces, and ceremonial headgear (adorned with hornbill feathers and wild boar tusks).   Cultural Transmission: Festive dances mimic martial arts, ancient battle movements, and celebratory victory chants, preserving their ancestral history for younger generations.   3. Social Cohesion & PeacekeepingStrengthening Kinship: Festivals serve as a reunion where families, clans, and neighboring villages set aside past rivalries.Reconciliation: Festivals such as Lingnyu Monyü were explicitly designed to forge non-aggression pacts, foster inter-village goodwill, and seal community alliances through shared feasts.4. title: Lotha Tribe
subtitle: Region: Wokha District · Festival: Tokhu Emong
content:
A Post-Harvest Festival of Thanksgiving, Reconciliation, and Rest. One of the most important festivals for the Lotha tribe.

Harvest Festival of Thanksgiving, Reconciliation, Unity and Forecasting. The Village Chief (Pvϋti), invites all the Chϋmpho-ramo e (leaders of the Dormitories) and its members, and in the midst of the gathering; the Chief launches the Tokhϋ Emong, by announcing the dates and the rituals required to be performed by all. Launching of Tokhϋ Emong, by the Pvϋti, is followed, in like manner by all the Chϋmpo leaders and thereby the whole village start to observe the rituals of Tokhϋ Emong. The main targets of Tokhϋ Emong are Thanksgiving; for the blessings during the passing year, Reconciliation and fostering unity, among the villagers, and forecasting the nature of the coming next year.

title: Rengma Tribe
subtitle: Region: Tseminyü District · Festival: 1. Ngada Festival (Post-Harvest Festival)
content:
The cultural significance of Rengma Naga traditional festivals—principally Ngada—goes far beyond simple celebration; it acts as the foundation of their identity, spirituality, governance, and social framework.   1. Agricultural Gratitude and TransitionGratitude for Survival: As an agrarian society, the harvest represents survival and prosperity. Ngada marks the end of the long agricultural year, allowing the community to express collective thanksgiving for the fruits of their hard labor before entering a period of winter rest.   Alignment with Nature: The festival signals the change of seasons and resets the agricultural calendar for the coming year.   2. Ancestral Honor and Spiritual ContinuityBridge Between the Living and the Dead: Rengmas hold a deep belief in keeping a strong bond with their departed ancestors. The ritual offering of food and drink on graves ensures that spirits are honored before they bid a final farewell to their earthly homes.   Spiritual Purification: Specific rites are performed to cleanse the village of ill fortune and ward off evil spirits, creating a clean slate for the community.   3. Social Harmony and ForgivenessReconciliation and Peace: A cornerstone of Rengma cultural philosophy during Ngada is resolving interpersonal disputes, family grudges, or inter-clan conflicts. It is culturally forbidden to harbor bad blood into the new year; all grievances are forgiven and forgotten through shared meals.Strengthening Kinship: Sharing home-brewed rice beer (Nkhezü) and festive food across households reinforces community unity, hospitality, and social egalitarianism.4. Preservation of Oral History and HeritageWarrior Legacy: The grand processions—where men dress in full traditional warrior attire (Rhikhu/Azachu shawls, hornbill feathers, boar-tusk ornaments)—keep the ancestral warrior heritage alive for younger generations.Oral Transmission: Folk songs (Ngada hwan), dances, and stories performed during the festival preserve the history, legends, and values of the Rengma people that are not recorded in written texts.5. Ecological Harmony and ProtectionPacts with Nature: The closing rites of Ngada feature symbolic "agreements" or rites made with fire (to prevent village fires) and rats/pests (to protect stored granaries). This reflects the tribe's traditional understanding of living in balance with their natural environment

The traditions surrounding the Ngada festival—the premier traditional festival of the Rengma Naga tribe—are deeply rooted in agricultural gratitude, ancestor reverence, and community harmony.

The core traditions and ritualistic practices that define Ngada include:

1. Ritual Remembrance of the Departed (Pfüchih)
Soul-Feeding Ceremony: A defining tradition of Ngada is the solemn remembrance of family members and ancestors who passed away during the year.

Symbolic Offerings: On the specific memorial day of the festival, family members carry small portions of cooked food, meat, and drops of local rice beer to the village outskirts or gravesides, offering a final meal to the departed souls before they transition to the spirit world.

2. The Festival Procession and Warrior Attire
Full Regalia: Men dress in their traditional warrior attire—including ceremonial hornbill-feathered headgear, brass armlets, boar-tusk ornaments, and distinct Rengma warrior shawls (Rhikhu or Azachu).

Community Marching: Accompanied by beating drums and gongs, villagers march through the streets singing traditional chants (Ngada hwan) that recount historical victories, legendary tales, and ancestral migration. Women join the procession carrying baskets filled with rice beer and feast items.

3. Forgiveness and Reconciliation Rites
Clearing the Slate: Ngada doubles as a time of total social restoration. By tradition, any lingering disputes, family feuds, or inter-personal quarrels from the past year must be settled before or during the festival.

Shared Feasting as a Pact: Sharing food and drinking rice beer together serves as a binding social contract that restores peace, friendship, and unity within the clan and village.

4. Closing Rituals and Protective Agreements (Tekang)
On the final day of the festival, elders perform sacred rites to safeguard the community for the upcoming year:

The Fire Pact: Prayers and rituals are performed to invoke protection against accidental village fires.

The Pest Protection Rite: Symbolic rites are held to ward off rats, insects, and wildlife that might threaten the newly stored grain in granaries.

Banishment of Evil: A final symbolic ritual is carried out to chase away malevolent spirits and invite health, abundance, and peace into the Rengma households.

Traditional Food and Drink
Rice Beer (Nkhezü): No ritual or feast is complete without the brewing and sharing of home-brewed rice beer, which is offered to guests, elders, and ancestors alike.

Community Meat Sharing: Pigs and cattle are ritually slaughtered, and the meat is systematically distributed among families and extended relatives according to traditional clan hierarchy.
